tagline.text: Cebu City's one-stop market for dried fish, danggit, and souvenirs

location.label: Location
location.text: San Nicolas, Cebu City (around Tres de Abril Street and Lakandula Street)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–2,500 (dried fish and snacks plus local transport; varies with how much you buy)

children.text: Taboan Public Market is a traditional market in San Nicolas, Cebu City, known as the place to buy pasalubong such as danggit, Cebu's signature dried fish, as well as dried squid and dried mangoes, at the lowest prices and with the widest selection. It is smelly and crowded, but early in the morning it has the most to offer.

Taboan Public Market is a traditional market in the San Nicolas district of Cebu City, with so many shops selling dried seafood that it is nicknamed the "buwad (dried fish) capital." For travelers it is known as a place where you can buy Cebu's signature souvenir, danggit (dried rabbitfish), along with dried squid, dried shrimp, dried mangoes, and sweets such as otap and rosquillos, all in one spot. The market is described as the block bounded by Tres de Abril, Lakandula, B. Aranas, and T. Padilla streets.

The market's beginnings go back to the aftermath of the Battle of Tres de Abril in Cebu on April 3, 1898. Spanish troops arrested most of San Nicolas's residents on suspicion of Katipunan membership, and many fled to the mountains. As the town recovered, a lot called Tagbu-an was set aside where city buyers and mountain producers could meet. A local newspaper column says this later came to be called Taboan. In other words, this market is not just a souvenir shop but a place where the everyday history of Cebu's people continues. There is also an anecdote that the sellers from the mountains were told not to cross a bridge called "Puti ug Pula" into other parts of the city, which kept trade concentrated in San Nicolas.

Much of the dried fish is said to come from Bantayan Island in the north. One guide says Bantayan has perfected the art of drying fish. Locals dip danggit in vinegar, add garlic or pepper, and eat it with rice. It is often already dried and boned, so it keeps well after you buy it, and many shops offer vacuum packing.

You should know about the strong smell, the narrow aisles, and the age of the building. In June 2025 there was a report that the San Nicolas barangay captain asked the city government for urgent repairs, saying that the market's second floor is structurally unsound. More than 100 stalls are said to operate there, but repair plans and open areas can change, so check the latest news before you go.

This is Cebu's signature dried fish. It comes salt-cured or marinated in garlic; the marinated kind has a stronger flavor and is the popular choice for pasalubong. Prices vary with size and season, so compare shops.

blocks.title: Dried squid and other dried fish

children.text: Dried squid, shredded squid, dilis, tuyo, espada, and other dried fish are piled up by type. There are also seasoned dried products such as fish tapa and tocino, and some shops let you taste before you choose.

Souvenirs such as dried mangoes, otap, rosquillos, peanut brittle, banana chips, garlic chips, local vinegar, and chili oil are sold here too. If the smell of dried fish bothers you, you can buy only these.
Many shops sell vacuum-packed products from 250 g to 1 kg, and some will vacuum-pack the fish you pick. Be sure to ask before loading it on a plane, and check the weight again after packing.

Besides dried fish, fruit, vegetables, fresh seafood, and meat are traded in this crowded market. You can see the daily life of Cebu's people up close, with sellers and shoppers coming and going from early on. More than 100 stalls are reported, and weekends and holidays are busier.
The story that the market arose after the Battle of Tres de Abril in 1898 ties in with the street name "Tres de Abril." Walking and noticing the street names lets you see the local history.

blocks.title: A walk through Cebu's city markets

children.text: Combine it with Carbon Market or Colon Street, on foot or by jeepney, for a half-day local route. Both markets are best early.

items.title: Half-day pasalubong route
items.subtitle: Morning market shopping and a stroll along Colon Street

children.text: Take a taxi or Grab from your hotel to Taboan Market. It is said to take about 15–20 minutes from Ayala Center and about 20–25 minutes from SM City Cebu.
Walk once around the dried fish shops, compare danggit sizes and prices, and ask whether you can taste.
Ask for the danggit and dried squid you bought to be vacuum-packed, and check the weight again.
Buy sweets such as dried mangoes, otap, and rosquillos, and sort out your cash.
Take a taxi or jeepney toward Colon Street and Carbon Market and have lunch.
The smell clings to clothes, so bring washable clothes and a spare bag.
Buy danggit and other dried fish at the market and ask for vacuum packing.
Return to your hotel and pack them in your luggage, or set them aside for carry-on.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant before heading to the airport.
Check the dried fish import rules of your destination before you leave.

items.title: Local route by jeepney
items.subtitle: Walk from Colon Street and ride back by jeepney

children.text: Have breakfast on Colon Street and look for a jeepney heading toward Taboan or San Nicolas. Route numbers change over the years, so ask the driver or a local.
Get off near the market entrance and start with the dried fish area. Some guides say it is a 10–15 minute walk, so on a nice day you can walk.
Make a list of what to buy and check your cash. Stalls mostly take cash, so bring cash in advance.
Gather your purchases in one big shopping bag and return to your hotel by jeepney or taxi. The smell of dried fish can spread to other passengers, so make sure it is well wrapped.
Jeepneys are inconvenient with lots of luggage, so take a taxi or Grab for large purchases.

The market is open year-round, and early morning is the most abundant and least crowded time. One guide says the selection is widest between 8 a.m. and noon, and another recommends going before 11 a.m.

Hours differ by source. Some guides say it is open from very early morning until 8 p.m., while an older guide says the dried fish shops start closing around 5 p.m., so arrive early in the afternoon at the latest. Prices may rise in December, January, and Holy Week, and weekends and holidays are busier.

Prices change with season and peak periods. One 2026 guide says marinated danggit costs about ₱400–500 per kilo in the dry season (January–May) and ₱500–600 in the rainy season (August–December), but that guide is hard to confirm independently, so treat it only as a reference and check on the spot.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Danggit prices are said to be relatively stable. Visit early in the morning.
Moisture and the smell of dried fish can be stronger, so bring an umbrella and a change of clothes.
Souvenir demand rises, so prices may go up and it can be crowded.

There are almost no places to stay right next to Taboan Market, so people usually come and go by taxi or Grab from downtown hotels. If you are only buying pasalubong, you can stay anywhere around Ayala Center, IT Park, or Colon Street and reach it in 15–30 minutes. Dried fish kept in your room can smell, so ask for vacuum packing and put it in an extra zip bag. Some hotels may not allow dried fish inside the rooms.

For food, snack lightly at the stalls inside the market and have lunch around Colon Street or Carbon Market, which is more convenient. A guide says there are no public restrooms in the market, so use one before you go and bring wet wipes or a spare T-shirt.

Good danggit is described as evenly golden in color, firm in flesh, and with a salty sea smell. Avoid anything that smells sour or like ammonia. Storage is given as 2–3 weeks at room temperature, about 1 month in the refrigerator, and up to 3 months in the freezer. The usual way to eat it is to fry it crisp and eat it with rice, dipping it in vinegar with garlic and pepper. Prices swing a lot over time: one 2011 report put danggit at around ₱700 per kilo, while recent guides give a range of ₱400–600. Sources differ, so compare several shops on the spot and bargain.
Go early in the morning for the widest choice and fewer crowds.
The price of danggit varies a lot with size and seasoning, so compare two or three shops.
If you buy 2 kg or more, ask for a discount.
Bring small bills (₱50, ₱100) to avoid problems with change.
Check the weight before and after packing. Some reviews mention short weighing.
On the plane, block the smell with vacuum packing or double plastic bags.
Dried fish import rules differ by country, so check them before you fly home.
Bring washable clothes, a spare bag, and wet wipes.
If you wonder how to eat it, ask the shop how to fry it. Serving it with vinegar and garlic is the usual way.
Dried fish left in your room can spread its smell, so vacuum-pack it and put it in a zip bag once more.
A June 2025 report said the market's second floor was pointed out as structurally unsafe. It is an old building, so follow safety signs in the aisles and on-site instructions.
The smell of dried fish stays on clothes and bags for a long time.
Beware of pickpockets in the crowded aisles and carry your bag in front.
Many shops have no price tags, so confirm the total before bargaining.
There are reviews of packages coming up short in weight, so check the scale.
Taxis and Grab are congested around the market, so it is easier to set your pickup point on a main road.
The roads near the market have many motorbikes and carts, so be careful when crossing, and after buying a lot your hands are full and it is easy to leave things behind.
